rv.q: Like some forgotten treasure found in the attic, the Old Vic‘s radiant revival of “The Winslow Boy” — now presented on Broadway by the Roundabout Theater — practically glows in the dark.
A trivial crime makes for delightful revival.
I can firmly state that the audience's ultimately is [rewarded].
The Winslow Boy is a beautifully written play about the price of principle, and it has been given a production worthy of its worth.

Directed for the screen by Anthony Asquith in 1948, and again by David Mamet in 1999, the play was last seen on Broadway 65 years ago. It's a slow starter, and indeed its unhurried four acts might seem to lack economy for contemporary audiences.

So many things onstage these days champion the notion that change is good - open your mind, learn to love what you fear, embrace the unknown. So it's refreshing to have something that cheers the hopelessly stubborn...
In Morton, Rattigan gives us (and Nivola thrillingly fulfills) a ham of a character whose vanity and control of his technique are so complete he might almost seem a villain out of melodrama.
Watching Parry and Nivola stiffly dance around each other’s feelings is melanchic and delightful.
Scrupulously acted and handsomely designed, the show vibrates with humor and genuine emotion.
Rees is bravura as a man physically falling apart yet spiritually revived.
Lindsay Posner's elegant staging heightens the spring-wound tension Rattigan skillfully builds.

So why waste any more time before declaring that what Rattigan advocates Haimes and Posner have worked out is one of the best productions on which the Roundabout has ever raised a curtain at the Theatre?
The failure to stage the climactic courtroom scene is actually one of Rattigan's finest touches.
The surprising humor, and the vibrant and detailed performances of the cast offer so much more juice than the more overtly relevant play.
The truth, while more complicated, is no harder to predict than any of the developments in Winslow Boy; but this winsome revival will charm you nonetheless.
But it appears that the beating heart of this piece was left on the other side of the pond.
This Old Vic production, directed by Lindsay Posner, is smart and gripping and not at all creaky.

cn.t: Critics praise this elegant, well-acted Rattigan revival for its compelling examination of principle and family honor, though some find the British period piece's deliberate pace demands patience from modern audiences.

sg.vl: Intimate 740-seat house, center orchestra is the premium pick
sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name center orchestra rows C-H (seats 105-109) as the best unobstructed views in the 740-seat house; rows E-J are called out as the value sweet spot before mezz overhang begins at row H. TripAdvisor reviewer: 'had great seats (row 3) ... seats further back would have been good too' given the small theater size.

sg.vl: Under deep mezz overhang, top of stage cut off
sg.ra: Headout guidance: 'Avoid the last three orchestra rows (N, O, and P) and the extreme corner seats.' Corroborated by search finding that beyond row N 'seats experience cut-off at the top of the stage' due to the mezzanine overhang that starts at row H.

sg.vl: Overhead sightline into the set, better-than-average legroom
sg.ra: Headout: 'Mezzanine seats as close to the middle of rows A to C as possible offer fantastic overhead views of the stage which are perfect for impressive sets and sweeping action.' Headout also notes 'better than average legroom, which makes up for the lack of inside aisles.' BWW forum poster recommended Mezz Row A seats 109-110 as a strong option.
sg.rr: A-G (single curved section, ~257 seats, no center aisle)

sg.vl: Budget-friendly with clean sightlines in a small house
sg.ra: Headout: 'rear mezzanine offers budget-friendly options with a pretty good view of the stage for a lower price.' TripAdvisor reviewer sat 'in the very last row of the balcony at this beautiful old theater and had an excellent view' — small-house intimacy holds up to the back wall.
sg.rr: D-G (within the single A-G mezz; back rows cited)

sg.vl: Heavily obstructed per TripAdvisor and BWW forum
sg.ra: TripAdvisor reviewer on house-wide sightlines: 'Most seats have excellent views of the stage, apart from the box seats labeled as obstructed view ... When this theater says obstructed, it means obstructed -- not partially obstructed.' BWW forum user tombomb31 on the box seats: 'I'm pretty sure I remember hearing they're incredibly obstructed.' Search notes: 'Anything that is on the far side of the stage you are sitting on is obstructed.'
